payload.original: Historical investigation recorded from primary sources. Outcome: success. Apollo 11 lifted off at 13:32:00 GMT on 16 July 1969, the lunar module landed at GET 102:45:40 on 20 July after five computer program alarms during powered descent, and the crew returned on 24 July [A11-C001, A11-C066, A11-C073, A11-C076]. This investigation does not posit a failure: it examines why a complex descent continued safely despite operational anomalies.
payload.title: Apollo 11 lunar landing, July 1969: why the descent succeeded despite program alarms

payload.original: The Mission Report defines all times as elapsed time from range zero, the integral second before lift-off, and gives range zero as 13:32:00 G.m.t., July 16, 1969. [A11-C001]
The translunar injection maneuver ignited at GET 02:44:16.2, and trajectory parameters after TLI were nearly perfect (velocity within 1.6 ft/sec of plan). [A11-C004]
Lunar orbit insertion ignition occurred at GET 75:49:50.4, placing the spacecraft into a 60- by 169.7-mile lunar orbit. [A11-C005]
Undocking of the LM from the CSM is listed at GET 100:12:00 in the Mission Report sequence of events. [A11-C006]
After reacquisition of signal, Armstrong reported the LM undocked: 'The Eagle has wings.' [A11-C007]
Descent orbit insertion ignition was at GET 101:36:14 and powered descent initiation (descent engine ignition) at GET 102:33:05.2. [A11-C008]
The first program alarm (1202) is listed as computer-determined at GET 102:38:22. [A11-C012]
Armstrong reported the first program alarm on air-to-ground. [A11-C016]
Armstrong identified the alarm code as 1202, echoed by Aldrin, and asked Houston for a reading on it. [A11-C017]
CAPCOM Charlie Duke gave the Go on the first 1202 alarm about half a minute after the alarm. [A11-C018]
The second 1202 alarm is listed at GET 102:39:02. [A11-C013]
Aldrin reported the second alarm as the 'same alarm' and correlated it with having the Verb 16 Noun 68 display up. [A11-C019]

The ground's real-time response to the second 1202 report was an acknowledgment ('Roger. Copy.') followed by an offer to monitor Delta-H; the transcript shows no explicit 'Go' word for this alarm. [A11-C020]
The 1201 alarm is listed as computer-determined at GET 102:42:18, after entry into P64 at 102:41:32. [A11-C014]
Aldrin reported the 1201 alarm; Duke replied that it was Go, the same type. [A11-C021]
Two further 1202 alarms are listed at GET 102:42:43 and 102:42:58 (both computer-determined). [A11-C015]
During P64 Duke acknowledged a later 1202 with 'Roger. 1202. We copy it.' This is an acknowledgment, not a Go call. [A11-C022]
Program P66 (rate-of-descent mode) was entered at GET 102:43:22 to reduce altitude rate and keep height for site surveillance. [A11-C050]
Table 5-I lists the red-line low-level sensor light at GET 102:44:28. [A11-C057]
Aldrin called five percent fuel remaining and the quantity light at 100 feet. [A11-C054]
Duke called '60 seconds'. [A11-C055]
Duke called '30 seconds'. [A11-C056]

The Mission Report gives lunar landing at GET 102:45:39.9 (Table 3-I) and 102:45:40 with engine off at the same time (Table 5-I); Aldrin's 'Contact Light' call is at 102:45:40 in the ALSJ transcript. [A11-C066]
Armstrong announced: 'Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed.' [A11-C067]
The Mission Report gives the commander's first contact with the lunar surface as 109:24:15 (9:56:15 p.m. e.s.t., July 20, 1969). [A11-C068]
Egress (hatch opening) was at GET 109:07:33 and ingress (hatch closing) at 111:39:13. [A11-C069]
CAPCOM Ron Evans passed the change to the crew: no rendezvous radar during ascent, to address the descent alarms. [A11-C082]
Evans framed the ascent radar-off change as a hedged working hypothesis: 'we think' it would take care of 'some of' the overflow. [A11-C102]
Aldrin pushed back that the rendezvous radar had been in Slew during descent. [A11-C103]
Aldrin told Houston from the surface that the rendezvous radar switch had been in Slew, not LGC, during descent. [A11-C038]
Lunar lift-off occurred on time at GET 124:22:00.8, into a 48.0- by 9.4-mile orbit. [A11-C070]
Docking occurred at GET 128:03:00; the rendezvous was successful with all guidance and control systems operating satisfactorily. [A11-C071]
Transearth injection ignition was at GET 135:23:42.3. [A11-C072]
Entry interface was at GET 195:03:05.7 and command module landing at 195:18:35, which the recovery table gives as 1650 G.m.t. on July 24. [A11-C073]
The crew, in biological isolation garments, were retrieved by helicopter to USS Hornet (crew aboard 1753 G.m.t., in the Mobile Quarantine Facility 1758 G.m.t.). [A11-C074]
The crew and spacecraft were released from quarantine on August 10, 1969, with no evidence of abnormal medical reactions; no microorganisms of extraterrestrial origin were recovered. [A11-C075]

payload.mechanism: With the rendezvous radar mode switch in AUTO or SLEW (the configuration the procedures called for; whether the procedure or the interface specification was at fault is contested), resolver excitation came from a 28-volt 800-hertz supply frequency-locked but not phase-locked to the guidance reference; the CDUs slewed and sent continuous pulses to the computer (A11-C031, A11-C032, A11-C033). Repetitive jobs were then scheduled again before earlier copies completed, overflowing the Executive (A11-C029, A11-C030, A11-C034): 1202 when no core sets and 1201 when no VAC areas were free, both Executive bailout alarms (A11-C118). The mechanism was established by post-flight analysis and simulation; on the surface it was a hedged working hypothesis (A11-C102).
payload.statement: The 1202 and 1201 alarms were Executive overflows caused by counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data units, which stole more than 10 percent of the computer's capacity.

In P63 the crew's Verb 16 Noun 68 monitoring display added computer load that reduced the remaining margin; in P64 the essential load plus landing-point redesignation processing left less than 10 percent margin.
The alarms indicated a failure of the lunar module guidance computer.
The alarms were caused by the crew deviating from procedure in setting the rendezvous radar switch.

payload.mechanism: Mission Report: when capacity is exceeded the computer generates a software restart and an Executive overflow alarm (A11-C034); the alarms did not degrade any primary guidance or control function (A11-C035); participant analysis describes the restarts shedding load (A11-C046, A11-C047).
payload.statement: The computer's restart protection preserved guidance: each overflow triggered a software restart that discarded stale jobs and resumed the priority guidance and control computations.

Flight controllers could judge in real time that the alarms were not a guidance failure, because it had been decided before flight that such alarms would not prevent continuing while they were intermittent and navigation was good; they gave explicit Go calls for the first 1202 and the 1201 and a general Go before the late 1202s.
Armstrong's manual control in P66 extended the range past a boulder field around a large crater to a safe touchdown point.

Propellant monitoring and callouts kept the landing inside the margin: the engine was cut off with about 45 s of firing time remaining against a 20 s landing go/no-go point, and post-flight calculation (50 s) agreed with the onboard indication within measurement accuracy.

A backup abort guidance system ran in monitor mode through descent and mission rules defined when the primary guidance had failed, so continuing after the alarms kept an abort path, although abort options narrowed close to the surface.

payload.mechanism: Doppler residuals showed the guidance estimate about 21,000 ft uprange; the dispersion was caused primarily by state-vector errors before PDI (A11-C010, A11-C011, A11-C052); manual control then extended range about 1100 ft (A11-C051).
payload.statement: The landing came long of its target mainly because the onboard state vector carried a downrange error at powered descent initiation, with manual range extension adding to it.
Eagle landed with only seconds of usable propellant to spare (a common popular framing).
The automatic descent would have reached a safe landing without crew intervention.

payload.mechanism: ANOMALY: counter interrupts from the rendezvous radar coupling data units, caused by unsynchronized 800-hertz excitation with the radar switch out of LGC, stole more than 10 percent of computer capacity (root cause of the alarms); monitoring displays reduced the remaining margin (contributing). CONTINUATION: restart protection kept the priority guidance computations running (enabling condition); controllers applied a pre-flight decision that such alarms did not stop the descent and gave Go; Armstrong flew P66 past a boulder field; propellant was monitored to touchdown inside the margin (contributing factors); backup abort guidance remained available though narrowing near the surface (enabling condition). LANDING POINT: a state-vector error at PDI put the descent long, toward the boulder field (contributing factor). The root-cause role refers to the alarms only; the other roles explain the continuation and the landing point. The single assertion combines the anomaly and its successful handling because the v1 cause gate does not allow a second, independent assertion beside it.
payload.outcome: Five executive-overflow program alarms occurred during Apollo 11's powered descent, and the descent nevertheless continued to a safe landing, long of its target

payload.residualUncertainty: Whether the procedure or the interface specification was at fault is contested; no source supports a crew deviation. The capacity figure differs by source (over 10, about 13, up to 15 percent). No single precise fuel-remaining figure is asserted; the Mission Report's 45 s / 50 s agreement is primary, the larger slosh margin is later commentary. The alarm-free ascent is consistent with the workaround but two changes were made together and it cannot show what would have happened without them. On the surface the radar cause was a hedged working hypothesis; the mechanism was established after the flight. Pairing of individual Go calls with alarms is partly uncertain. The flown effect of the Luminary 1B software correction is not in the retrieved Apollo 11 record.
payload.statement: Apollo 11 succeeded. The five 1202/1201 alarms during powered descent were Executive overflows caused by rendezvous radar coupling data unit interrupts that stole more than 10 percent of the computer's capacity; they did not degrade guidance or control. The descent continued because restart protection kept the priority guidance running, controllers applied a pre-flight decision that such intermittent alarms did not stop the descent and gave Go, Armstrong flew P66 past a boulder field (the descent had come in long because of a state-vector error at PDI) and cut off the engine with about 45 s of firing time remaining against a 20 s go/no-go point, and backup abort guidance remained available. The Mission Report lists no program alarms in ascent, which flew with the revised checklist package; this is consistent with the workaround but does not prove it. The causal roles apply to two effects: the root cause explains the alarms, the other members explain the continuation and the landing point.

payload.reason: The Luminary 1B software correction needs evidence from later missions, outside the retrieved Apollo 11 record; the ascent workaround met its criterion (no ascent alarms recorded) but is not the root-cause correction.
